annotations.keyFindings: Professional interpretation was linked to better patient-reported understanding in 10 of 14 studies; ad hoc interpreters made clinically significant errors in 22 percent of utterances against 12 percent for professionals.
annotations.limitations: Small observational primary studies; outcomes too varied to pool.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 11 studies, accuracy and satisfaction were similar for video and in-person interpretation; understanding was measured in only three small studies, and no study was designed to show equivalence.
annotations.limitations: Few studies measured understanding; video problems in 9 to 18 percent of sessions.

annotations.keyFindings: Without professional interpretation, odds of 30-day readmission were higher (odds ratio 1.3, 95 percent CI 1.1 to 1.6) across 21 observational studies; understanding was not measured.
Recall of consent information was better with a professional interpreter in five of seven studies that measured it.
annotations.limitations: Cross-sectional single-site studies; short-term recall only.

annotations.keyFindings: Patient-reported understanding was measured in only 9 of 38 discharge communication studies.
annotations.limitations: Scoping review; no quality appraisal of included studies.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 19 reviews, three were rated high confidence and 11 critically low; primary study overlap was substantial (corrected covered area 18 percent).
annotations.limitations: Methods study of reviews to its search date.

annotations.keyFindings: Tested bilingual staff made fewer errors than untested staff; untested staff often overestimated their proficiency.
annotations.limitations: Small single-hospital studies; understanding rarely measured.

claims.text: Professional interpretation was associated with better patient-reported understanding in 10 of 14 comparative studies, and ad hoc interpreters made clinically significant errors in 22 percent of utterances against 12 percent for professionals.
claims.passage: Professional interpretation was associated with better patient-reported understanding of diagnosis or treatment in 10 of the 14 studies.
claims.interpretation: Supports a standard favouring professional interpreters; the primary studies are small.

claims.passage: No included study was designed to show that video and in-person interpretation are equivalent for understanding.
claims.interpretation: The claim that video is as good as in-person for understanding is not established by the retrieved reviews.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, six of them reviews and one a methods study of reviews, appraised at abstract level. Reviews agree that professional interpretation is associated with better understanding and fewer errors than ad hoc interpretation, although the primary studies are small. For video against in-person interpretation, accuracy and satisfaction look similar, but understanding was measured in only three small studies and no study was designed to show equivalence. Understanding is rarely measured in discharge and consent studies, and outcome studies such as readmission are confounded. A methods study found most reviews in this field critically low in confidence with heavy overlap of the same primary studies, so counting agreeing reviews would overstate the evidence. An umbrella review must rate review quality and handle overlap.
gradeRationale: Reviews of small observational studies with heavy overlap and mostly critically low review quality; consistent direction for professional versus ad hoc interpretation but very limited evidence on patient-reported understanding by mode. Certainty is low overall and very low for video versus in-person understanding.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; certainty low.
